opus-5.5.text:
I think what struck me about Seedance is that it doesn't feel like a demo anymore. For a long time, video generation was a field where you'd see a really beautiful five-second clip, and then you'd try it yourself and realize that clip was the one in a hundred that worked. With Seedance, the floor got raised, not just the ceiling. The average output is coherent. Motion is physically plausible, the camera moves like a real camera, and when there are multiple shots, the characters and the scene stay consistent across cuts. That last part is actually really hard, and it's the thing that makes it usable for storytelling rather than just eye candy.

The second thing, honestly, is the engineering. People in academia, and I include myself, sometimes underestimate how much of this progress is about the whole system: data curation, captioning, the training recipe, the inference efficiency, the post-training to align with what humans actually find good. Seedance feels like a team that took every one of those pieces seriously at the same time. There isn't one magic trick; it's a thousand small decisions done well. That's very impressive to me, and a little humbling.

And third, from a research perspective, it makes me think about what these models are actually learning. When a video model can keep an object permanent behind an occlusion, or make water splash in a way that looks right, you start to ask: is there some implicit world model in there? I don't think it's a full world model. It still makes mistakes that no human would make, and it's still mostly optimized to look right rather than be right. But the fact that we can even have that debate seriously now is a sign of how far things have come. So for me Seedance is impressive both as a product and as a kind of scientific signal about where visual intelligence might be heading.

fable-5.1.text:
Saining Xie: Honestly, when I first saw the Seedance results I had the same reaction a lot of people had, which was that moment of "wait, is this real footage?" And I think that's actually the least interesting part of it. Photorealism alone doesn't impress me anymore; we've known for a while that diffusion models can produce beautiful frames.

What impressed me is the temporal coherence and the physics. Watch a Seedance clip with a camera pan across a room, and the geometry stays consistent. Objects occlude and reappear the way they should. Fabric moves, liquids pour, hands interact with objects without melting into them. Those are the things that broke almost every earlier video model, and they break because the model doesn't actually have a stable internal representation of the 3D world. So when I see those failure modes largely gone, that tells me something about representation learning is happening inside the model that goes well beyond pattern-matching pixels.

The second thing is the multi-shot narrative control. You can give it a prompt that implies a cut, a change in camera angle, a character moving between scenes, and it keeps identity and lighting consistent across shots. From a research perspective that's hard. It means the model is maintaining something like a scene state across time, not just extending the previous frame.

And the third thing, which is more personal to me, is what it says about scaling. I've spent a lot of my career thinking about architectures: ConvNeXt, DiT, how transformers should be structured for visual data. Seedance is evidence that when you get the data pipeline right and scale a diffusion transformer carefully, the capabilities you get are qualitatively different from what you'd expect by extrapolating the loss curve. It's the same lesson language models taught us, but seeing it in video, where the data is so much more raw and unstructured, makes me think vision models might be closer to becoming genuine world models than I would have predicted two years ago.

So I'm impressed less as a consumer and more as someone who sees it as a signal about where representation learning in vision is heading.

astra-6.text:
What impresses me is the sense that it’s generating a coherent scene, not just a sequence of beautiful frames. With video, everything has to work together: motion, timing, the camera, and the identity of the subject. A single frame can look convincing, but as soon as things move, inconsistencies become obvious.

Seedance is exciting to me because of how those pieces come together. It makes you think beyond image quality and ask: how much of the structure of the visual world can these models actually learn? I wouldn’t equate a convincing video with understanding physics, but that’s the research question that makes this so interesting.

sol-6.1.text: What impresses me is the consistency over time. Generating a beautiful frame is one thing, but making a scene move coherently—keeping the subject recognizable, the motion natural, and the camera movement connected to what’s happening—is much harder. With Seedance, those pieces seem to come together. You start paying attention to the scene itself instead of looking for where the generation breaks. To me, that’s a meaningful step toward making video generation a useful creative tool.
